title: The Tantalizing Possibility Of Locating Consciousness In The Brain | NOEMA
gist: An MIT Lincoln Laboratory neuroscientist argues that AI chatbots' human-like cognition without biological neurons undercuts the assumption that consciousness requires higher cognition, and proposes that subjective experience is instead a combinatorial, evolutionarily ancient signal generated by subcortical brain structures for arbitrating competing biological needs — with the cortex merely supplying that older system with richer information.

insights.claim: Modern chatbots' architecture was inspired by the neocortex, so their human-like behavior in language, abstraction, social inference and humor should not have been a complete surprise, but what few anticipated was that such complex behavior could emerge in the complete absence of biological neurons.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Suggests intelligence and cognitive behavior may be substrate-independent — implementable in silicon, biology, or in principle any sufficiently complex computational system — a claim with direct bearing on how much cognitive capability AI labs can expect to extract from architecture alone.
insights.quote: what few anticipated was that such complex behavior could emerge in the complete absence of biological neurons.
insights.locator: The design of modern chatbots was inspired by the neocortex

insights.claim: The mainstream position in neuroscience holds that cognition is a necessary ingredient of consciousness, yet the emergence of AI systems that achieve sophisticated cognitive feats without any accompanying claim to subjective experience undermines that assumption and reframes the central question from whether machines can experience anything to what kind of phenomenon consciousness is if it isn't fundamentally tied to higher cognition.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-consciousness debate away from 'can chatbots be conscious' toward a more foundational question about what consciousness actually is, which matters for how seriously AI welfare or moral-status claims should be taken given current systems.

insights.locator: The mainstream position in neuroscience is that cognition is a necessary ingredient of consciousness

insights.claim: Neurologist Antonio Damasio studied patients with damage to prefrontal cortex regions critical for emotional valuation who retained normal intelligence and reasoning but lost the ability to make decisions; one such patient, presented with two possible appointment times, was paralyzed with indecision, spending hours considering the question because the emotional signals that assign value to options had been disrupted.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Provides a clinical case showing that intelligence and decision-making are dissociable — reasoning alone, without an emotional valuation system, is insufficient for functional agency, a caution for AI systems designed around pure cognitive/reasoning capability.
insights.quote: When presented with two possible appointment times, the patient was paralyzed with indecision, spending hours considering the question.
insights.locator: One of Damasio's most cited patients

insights.claim: Damasio's 1994 book 'Descartes' Error' argued that feelings are not peripheral to rational thought but are part of the machinery that makes rational thought possible, a foundational reframe underlying later theories that human cognition emerges from combinations of primitive feeling states.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Establishes the intellectual foundation for treating emotion as a computational component of cognition rather than a separate, dispensable layer — relevant to debates over whether AI systems need affect-like mechanisms to reason robustly.

themes.theme: A Combinatorial Model of Subjective Experience

insights.claim: Freeman proposes that complex thoughts and mental states may be combinatorial assemblies of a finite number of primitive feeling states — for example, 'understanding' might be two parts familiarity and one part coherence, and 'hope' might be three parts anticipation and one part motivation — analogous to ingredients combining like a recipe, rather than requiring an endless catalogue of irreducible mental states.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Offers a testable, tractable model for how the brain could generate the richness of human thought from a small basis set, a framework that could inform AI architectures aiming to model affect-like internal states more efficiently.
insights.quote: Let’s say that two parts familiarity and one part coherence produce the thing we call “understanding.” Three parts anticipation and one part motivation produce a thing we call “hope.”
insights.locator: Now suppose that complex thoughts are assembled from these primitive felt states

insights.claim: If conscious experience is built from roughly 30 independent experiential dimensions with about 8 distinguishable levels each, the resulting space would contain roughly 1 octillion (10^27) possible configurations, whereas even if every human who has ever lived experienced a new conscious state three times per second for their entire lifetime, humanity would collectively have sampled only about 1 sextillion (10^21) experiences — roughly one-millionth of the available experiential landscape.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how vast the theoretical space of possible conscious experience is relative to what humanity has actually explored, illustrating why the richness of subjective experience doesn't require an implausibly large number of distinct irreducible mental states.
insights.quote: if every human who has ever lived experienced a new conscious state three times every second throughout their entire lifetime, humanity would collectively sample only about 1 sextillion (1021) experiences
insights.locator: Imagine that conscious experience is built from 30 independent experiential dimensions

themes.theme: Localizing Consciousness: Cortex vs. Subcortical Structures

insights.claim: Beginning in the 1920s, physiologists surgically removed the cerebral cortices from dozens of cats, and more recently genetically modified mice have been born without cortices; both groups of animals that survived were surprisingly capable, able to eat, reproduce, swim, groom themselves and even learn simple mazes, suggesting a cortex is not strictly necessary for at least some form of experience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Direct empirical evidence that basic behavioral competence — and plausibly some form of experience — can persist without the cortex, supporting the article's central claim that consciousness may be seated in older subcortical structures rather than the seat of higher cognition.

insights.claim: Deep-brain stimulation in humans can evoke intense subjective experiences, whereas stimulation of large regions of the prefrontal cortex often produces little or no conscious effect, supporting the hypothesis that the neural circuitry mediating subjective experience may sit in evolutionarily older subcortical structures rather than the cortex.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable neurological finding that directly supports relocating the search for the neural basis of consciousness away from the cortex, the field's traditional focus, toward more anatomically discrete subcortical targets.

insights.claim: Because subcortical structures are more anatomically discrete than the cortex's expansive, distributed networks, if consciousness is located there the search for its neural basis narrows from the sprawling cortical landscape to a relatively small, more tractable piece of neural anatomy — a discovery Freeman calls among the most consequential possible in neuroscience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: This is the article's central, highest-conviction claim: a smaller, more tractable anatomical target for consciousness research would make the search for the neural basis of subjective experience dramatically more feasible — a research-agenda-defining prediction for the field.
insights.quote: Structures deep within the brain are more anatomically discrete than the expansive networks of the cerebral cortex.
insights.locator: Here is where it gets especially interesting

insights.claim: Paraphrasing neuroscientist Bjorn Merker, Freeman suggests the cortex may generate the contents of consciousness — what we think about — while older deep-brain structures generate conscious experience itself, that we experience anything at all.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: A crisp division of labor between cortex and subcortex that reframes what AI systems modeled on the cortex (like transformer-based LLMs) can and cannot be expected to replicate about subjective experience.

themes.theme: Why Feelings Exist: An Evolutionary Function

insights.claim: If subjective experience were merely a passive readout of neural computation — like an aircraft instrument panel that reports but doesn't control the underlying machinery — it would be an evolutionary epiphenomenon, which is difficult to reconcile with evolution's tendency to eliminate biological functions that don't improve survival outcomes.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Sets up the article's functional theory of consciousness by using evolutionary logic to rule out a purely epiphenomenal account, which matters for whether any information-processing system (biological or artificial) that merely reports its internal state would count as conscious.

insights.locator: Taken literally, the idea that conscious experience is like the instrument panel

insights.claim: Freeman proposes feelings function as the brain's common currency for arbitrating competing biological priorities — eat or flee, rest or explore — with ancient upper-brainstem and hypothalamic structures converting incompatible physiological needs into a shared subjective signal that determines which action gets taken.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Gives consciousness a specific evolutionary function (motivational arbitration) rather than treating it as inert, which is the article's proposed answer to why subjective experience would have been preserved by natural selection at all.
insights.quote: Feelings are not merely reports about the state of the organ
insights.locator: Feelings are not merely reports about the state of the organism

themes.theme: Bringing Consciousness Research Into Mainstream Neuroscience

insights.claim: Consciousness research has not yet converged on a common framework for evaluating competing ideas, and researchers disagree not only about the answer but about the question itself, as illustrated by MIT researchers spanning anesthesiologist Emery Brown, electrophysiologist Earl Miller, and philosopher Matthias Michel, each approaching the mystery with different methods and assumptions.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Documents the field's current fragmentation, explaining why a claimed discovery about the neural basis of consciousness would still face a steep credibility barrier even if empirically well-supported.

insights.locator: A walk across MIT's campus illustrates the point

insights.claim: Freeman predicts that as theories become more firmly grounded in testable neural mechanisms, such as non-invasive deep-brain stimulation, the boundary between consciousness research and mainstream neuroscience may gradually dissolve, shifting the field from philosophy-dominated debate to a mechanistic branch of neuroscience.
insights.speaker: DANIEL FREEMAN
insights.so_what: Forecasts a methodological shift for an entire research field, relevant to how funders and institutions (including MIT's interdisciplinary consciousness initiative the author is helping build) might prioritize investment in mechanistic tools over philosophical debate.
